Eastern whipbird (Psophodes olivaceus) eggs, based on reported dimensions of 27 millimeters in length and 19.4 millimeters in width, yield an estimated initial wet mass of 5.32 grams [Ww0 = 5.32 grams] for the neonate following hatching. This relatively modest starting mass is typical for incubating bird eggs and underlies the subsequent growth trajectory. When eggs are incubated under controlled conditions maintaining a temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], a consistent developmental period of 17 days [ab = 17 days] until hatching is observed, a duration that reflects the thermal optimum for embryonic development in this species. Newly emerged nestlings are altricial and entirely dependent on parental provisioning for warmth and nutrition, displaying the characteristic pin-feathered appearance of a developing chick. The initial body mass provides a baseline from which the substantial mass gain required to reach adult dimensions can be assessed, and it represents a critical life-history parameter for understanding postnatal growth rates and energetic demands placed on the provisioning adults.

Considerable sexual size dimorphism is evident in adult body masses for this species. Females attain a maximum adult body mass of 56 grams [Wwi = 56 grams], a figure that likely reflects the energetic constraints of egg production and incubation. Males, in contrast, reach a greater ultimate wet weight of 68.2 grams [Wwi = 68.2 grams], a disparity that may be linked to enhanced competitive ability in territory defense and mate acquisition, roles that are often pronounced in birds with complex vocal displays such as the whipbird's characteristic song. These asymptotic mass values are derived from field measurements of breeding individuals and represent the plateau in somatic growth typical of reproductively active adults. The difference in mass between the sexes is a notable feature of the species' life history, influencing foraging ecology, metabolic rates, and parental care dynamics. This dimorphism establishes a clear benchmark for assessing individual condition and reproductive potential within the population.

At the physiologically active body temperature characteristic of passerine birds, approximately 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the basal metabolic rate of the Eastern whipbird was measured at 127.2 milliliters per hour [JOi = 127.2 milliliters per hour]. This oxygen consumption value provides a key energetic baseline for the species, representing the minimal cost of sustaining vital physiological functions under thermoneutral conditions. The measurement, obtained from respirometry trials on post-absorptive, resting adults during their inactive phase, situates the whipbird's metabolic rate within the expected range for an insectivorous passerine of its body size. This energetic datum is essential for constructing daily energy budgets and for understanding how the species allocates resources to thermoregulation, foraging, and, crucially, reproductive activities. It serves as a fundamental physiological currency against which other life-history traits, such as growth rates and reproductive output, can be meaningfully compared.

Under the same sustained thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the Eastern whipbird displays a characteristic sequence of developmental and reproductive milestones. The altricial nestling attains the ability to fledge from the nest at 12 days after hatching [tx = 12 days after hatching], a period consistent with the 10 to 13 day range reported for many related insectivorous species at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Subsequently, gonadal maturation occurs, with the onset of puberty, defined by the capacity for gamete production, being reached at 36 days after hatching [tp = 36 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Despite this relatively early physiological capability, first successful breeding is typically deferred, with evidence indicating that the time since birth at first brood is 401 days [tR = 401 days], suggesting a delay between sexual maturation and actual reproduction. at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]This delay is a common life-history strategy, allowing young birds to acquire territory, develop foraging proficiency, and build the body condition necessary for the substantial energetic investment of nesting.

The species' maximum recorded lifespan in the wild under the prevailing thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] is approximately 4,307 days [am = approximately 4,307 days], or nearly 11.8 years, a longevity that is appreciable for a passerine of this size. This extended lifespan allows for multiple breeding seasons and is often linked to a slower-paced life-history strategy characterized by relatively low annual reproductive output. Field surveys of reproductive activity show that females produce a clutch of 1 to 3 eggs per nesting attempt [N_R_i = 1 to 3 eggs per nesting attempt], and they typically complete approximately 2 to 3 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 clutches per year]. This low clutch frequency, combined with the small brood size, translates to a modest maximum reproductive rate, which is balanced by the species' high adult survival and long reproductive lifespan. Such demographic parameters are characteristic of birds that inhabit stable environments and invest heavily in parental care, ensuring the success of the few offspring they produce each season.
